clue.text: Weed: the first logical step preceding mild agricultural disaster

blocks.note: going from A to B is the proverbial first step in reasoning
mild, as in a light flavour or a light breeze

explanation.surface: A wry chain of reasoning: smoking weed is the start of a slide into a small farming catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weed' at the front looks like the definition, but it is slang for marijuana and starts the wordplay. POTATO BLIGHT is the fungus behind the Irish famine.
explanation.definitionFit: Potato blight is a crop disease that destroys whole harvests, a classic example of farming catastrophe.

clue.text: Irrational fellows to make pepper

blocks.note: pi is the best-known irrational number

explanation.surface: Unreasonable men out to produce a pepper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' is an adjective standing for a noun here: pi, the classic irrational number.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimento is a sweet red pepper, the kind stuffed into olives.

clue.text: Doctor slices fish in treeless plain

indicators.note: a blade that slices goes into the middle of something, so one piece sits inside the other

explanation.surface: A surgeon filleting fish out on the frozen plains.
explanation.definitionFit: Tundra is the flat, frozen Arctic land where trees cannot grow.

clue.text: "Git Along" covers, one of many for the Eagles

definitions.text: one of many for the Eagles

indicators.note: the quoted title covers the answer, holding it inside its letters

blocks.note: inside the title, spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Cover versions of a country song, one in a long list by the rock band the Eagles.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the band; the definition means the birds, each of which has several claws.
explanation.definitionFit: A talon is a claw of a bird of prey, and an eagle has many of them.

clue.text: Like a cowboy, perhaps, entreated to swallow a bird

indicators.note: to swallow is to take inside, so one word goes into the other

explanation.surface: A cowboy who pleaded to swallow a bird, as in some tall tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the cowboy as an example: long riding is said to bend the legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowlegged describes legs curving outward at the knee, the stereotype of a cowboy after years in the saddle.

clue.text: I can cope with a fart, as long as it exists in theory

blocks.note: to cope with something is to deal with it
a fart is a passing of gas

explanation.surface: Someone tolerant of flatulence, provided it is only hypothetical.
explanation.walkthrough: An ideal gas is the physicist's model whose molecules take up no space and never attract: no real gas behaves exactly so.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal gas is a theoretical model in physics, real only on paper.

clue.text: "The Bottom of the Dress" and "Pooh and Eeyore's Tails," by Alan Alexander (however, one is late)

indicators.note: a tail is the hind end, so each name gives its final letter
being late means arriving after the expected time, so the single letter moves further back

blocks.note: A. A. Milne, Alan Alexander, the author of Winnie-the-Pooh

explanation.surface: Two mock book titles credited to the author of the Pooh stories.
explanation.walkthrough: The author's surname has its I (the 'one') shifted one place later, after the L.
explanation.definitionFit: A hemline is the lower edge of a skirt or dress, its folded and sewn bottom.

clue.text: The Puebla-Hidalgo border is nothing special

indicators.note: the border between the two places is where their names meet, and the letters there make the word

explanation.surface: The frontier between two Mexican states is unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: Puebla and Hidalgo are neighbouring states of Mexico.
explanation.definitionFit: Blah is an informal word for dull or unremarkable.

clue.text: That guy had supported nicer bananas, with vitamins added

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: he'd, the contraction of he had

explanation.surface: A man who backed friendlier bananas, fortified with vitamins.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, a piece that supports another sits beneath it, so the contraction goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Enriched food has nutrients put back in, as with enriched flour.

clue.text: Panetta eats medium-size fruit

indicators.note: whoever eats something takes it inside, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: Leon Panetta, US Defense Secretary and CIA director
M is the clothing-size abbreviation for medium

explanation.surface: A politician snacking on a moderately sized piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Leon Panetta served as US Secretary of Defense; his first name wraps the size letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemon is a sour yellow citrus fruit.

clue.text: Language heard in section of the theater with fur

indicators.note: heard means we go by how the words are said, not by their spelling

blocks.note: a loge is a box or front balcony section in a theater
ermine is the white winter fur of the stoat

explanation.surface: A spoken tongue overheard in a theater box among patrons wearing furs.
explanation.walkthrough: Said together, loge and ermine run into one sound close to the name of the tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Low German is the family of dialects spoken in northern Germany, a recognised language in its own right.

clue.text: Obstacle concealed competition around noon both times

indicators.note: around says the outer words are wrapped about something placed in them

blocks.note: the noon letter used a second time, as these words ask

explanation.surface: An obstacle course race run around midday, twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both times' tells you the noon letter goes into each of the two words, HI(N)D and RA(N)CE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hindrance is something that gets in the way, the same thing as an obstacle.

clue.text: Italian man: American soldier follows him in France

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: An American soldier trailing an Italian man across France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follows' puts the soldier after the French pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi is a common Italian given name for a man.

clue.text: Summary dismissal to express disapproval before start of trimester

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

explanation.surface: A student thrown out after being jeered just as the term began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' belongs with 'express disapproval': the whole phrase is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the boot is an idiom for being fired or thrown out without ceremony.

clue.text: Simpsons character takes a bow with a diagram for a statistics class

definitions.text: a diagram for a statistics class

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a bow is a curved shape, an arch

explanation.surface: A cartoon boy taking a bow after presenting a chart in his stats lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes a bow' sounds like accepting applause; here bow means a curve.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar chart shows quantities as bars of different lengths, a staple graph of introductory statistics.

clue.text: Embargo clearing quiet nation

blocks.note: an embargo is a ban on trade

explanation.surface: A trade embargo that silences a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clearing' reads as a verb (an embargo clearing the way) but is the noun for an open space in a forest.
explanation.definitionFit: Bangladesh is a country in South Asia, so it is a nation.

clue.text: A university cat and a jerk with a gun

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: A campus cat and an idiot carrying a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' suggests an obnoxious person, but it means a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: An automatic is a self-loading firearm that fires repeatedly, such as a pistol.

clue.text: The narcs busted purse thief

indicators.note: something busted is broken apart, so its letters are put back in a new order

explanation.surface: Drug squad officers arrest a bag thief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busted' plays on police slang for arrested; narcs are narcotics agents.
explanation.definitionFit: A snatcher grabs bags and runs, so a purse thief is a bag snatcher.

clue.text: Foul grit inside is supposed to provide a lift?

definitions.text: is supposed to provide a lift?

indicators.note: foul suggests something fouled up or messed about, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Dirty grit stuck inside something meant to give you a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'a rising tide lifts all boats' is what makes the definition work; the question mark flags the playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising tide is said to lift all boats, the proverb for general prosperity helping everyone.

clue.text: Saint overseeing the rise of inner spirit's endurance

indicators.note: in a down answer a rise runs from bottom to top, so the word is read upward

blocks.note: the anima, Jung's term for the inner soul

explanation.surface: A saint guiding someone's spiritual growth and staying power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overseeing' puts the saint on top, first in a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the staying power to keep going, the same thing as endurance.

clue.text: Behold commercial cargo

blocks.note: lo, an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Look at that freight being advertised.
explanation.definitionFit: A load is the goods a vehicle or ship carries, which is what cargo means.

clue.text: How the lucky gambler might order his sandwich?

definitions.text: How the lucky gambler might order his sandwich?

blocks.note: a gambler in a winning streak, an idiom for success that keeps coming
the same phrase as a deli order: the filling served in a bread bun

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: a hot streak at the tables, and asking for your sandwich in a bun.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a roll is an idiom for a run of success, and a roll is also the bread for a sandwich.

clue.text: Hothead accompanies insanely nervy monarch

indicators.note: insanely means wildly, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: read as hot's head, the first letter of hot

explanation.surface: A hot-tempered person escorts a jittery king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hothead' looks like one word for a firebrand, but it splits into hot and its head; the answer is a king with a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry V was the English king who won at Agincourt.

clue.text: Someone close to mine is a dear (or sounds like a deer)

definitions.text: Someone close to mine is a dear

blocks.clueFragment: Someone close to mine is a dear
blocks.note: a dear ... is a beloved person, someone close to my own ...
said aloud it matches the old word for a male red deer

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a homophone hint: a hart is a stag, pronounced the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Heart is the tender term for a beloved person, as in 'dear heart'.

clue.text: Surrealism: two auxiliaries act up

indicators.note: something surreal is distorted out of its normal shape, so the word it is fused to comes out jumbled

blocks.note: the word read as surreal ism: the last three letters are the ones used
be and have, two auxiliary verbs of English

explanation.surface: An art-world note: two helper verbs in a Dali painting start playing up.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the first word as surreal ism: the ism is made surreal, its letters scrambled. Be and have are the auxiliaries that help form tenses.
explanation.definitionFit: To misbehave is to behave badly, the same as acting up.

clue.text: We might have it with our coffee and newspaper, you and me, after getting up

definitions.text: We might have it with our coffee

indicators.note: getting up in a down answer means rising from the bottom, so the letters are read upward

blocks.note: a rag is a low-grade newspaper
you and me together are us

explanation.surface: A breakfast routine: coffee, the paper and the two of us, once we're out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After getting up' paints the morning scene, but it signals reading the pieces upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar is what many people stir into their coffee, so we might take it with our cup.

clue.text: Princely family playing the odds in easy trek

indicators.note: the odds are the odd-numbered places, so only the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th are kept

explanation.surface: A noble household gambling on a gentle hike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing the odds' sounds like betting, but here it means taking the odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Este were a princely dynasty ruling Ferrara and Modena during the Italian Renaissance.

clue.text: Put out the cigars where some legislators are in session

definitions.text: where some legislators are in session

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed or thrown into disorder, so the letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: A smoking ban in a parliament: extinguish the cigars while the chamber sits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like stubbing out cigars, but it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reichstag building in Berlin houses the Bundestag, Germany's parliament, when it sits.

clue.text: Knievel leaving Franklin to settle down

indicators.note: when one person is leaving another, the first goes away, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: Evel Knievel, the American motorcycle stuntman

explanation.surface: A daredevil stuntman departing from a president's company in order to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the stuntman's first name from the president's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds roost when they come to rest for the night, so to roost is to settle.

clue.text: Savage eating cereal, with extravagant praise for a composer

indicators.note: eating takes food inside, so the outer word swallows what follows

explanation.surface: A harsh critic tearing into a breakfast cereal while gushing about a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the cereal and the praise, and both go inside the verb for savaging.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice Ravel was the French composer of Bolero.
